screens.title: Decision Making & Utility AI
screens.subtitle: Score, compare, and choose actions that feel smart and contextual

narration.text: In this lesson we will learn why Utility AI is a powerful alternative to purely reactive systems. Reactive approaches like finite state machines and simple behavior trees are straightforward, but they often force designers into brittle 'if-then' flows. Utility AI treats decision-making as a prioritization problem: each action is given a numerical utility based on the agent's current context, and the highest scoring action runs. You'll see how Considerations convert raw game data—health, distance, ammo—into normalized scores using curves or functions, and how those scores combine into an action's utility. We'll walk through the Unity implementation pattern that uses ScriptableObjects for Considerations and Actions, and a Decision Maker loop that evaluates options on an interval and executes the best one. I will also show a concrete example: an NPC that chooses between attack, heal, and flee based on its health and the player's distance. Finally, we'll consider practical trade-offs: how tuning curves affects behavior, why debugging score outputs matters, and where Utility AI is a better fit than an FSM. Think about a situation in your game where many factors should influence a single choice—that’s the space where Utility AI earns its keep.

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: Utility AI scores actions by usefulness in context, enabling nuanced, multi-factor decisions instead of brittle state switches.

Consider how each objective maps to a step in building and tuning the system so you can measure progress as you implement.

screens.title: Reactive Systems vs. Utility AI
screens.subtitle: Why purely reactive designs struggle with multi-factor decisions

narration.text: Reactive systems such as finite state machines and basic behavior trees make decisions by following explicit states or flows. These models are excellent when behavior is naturally segmented into distinct modes—for instance, an enemy that is either patrolling or chasing. But when many variables interact, an FSM can explode in complexity: each combination of factor conditions may need its own state or transition. Utility AI reframes the problem. Instead of encoding every possible situation, it evaluates candidate actions and assigns each a numerical utility reflecting how desirable that action is right now. For example, a squad leader deciding whether to attack, heal, or retreat doesn't just check a single flag; it weighs the unit's health, distance to allies, enemy strength, and available reinforcements. Concretely, an FSM would require states for low health + enemy near + low ammo, while a Utility AI would compute scores for Heal, Attack, and Retreat compositions and pick the highest. A common misconception is that Utility AI simply replaces states with numbers and is inherently more expensive; while it can be costlier, proper interval evaluation and relevance checks make it practical. Consider which approach fits your gameplay: use FSMs where clear states dominate, and prefer Utility when many graded factors must be balanced to produce believable choices.

keyIdea.title: Why choose Utility AI
keyIdea.text: Choose Utility AI when decisions require balancing multiple continuous factors rather than flipping discrete states.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.6 › Reactive vs Utility
Reactive
Finite State Machines
  • Clear states and transitions make behavior easy to visualize.
  • Works well when behaviors are mutually exclusive and simple.
  • Risk: state explosion when many interacting variables exist.
Common mistake
Trying to encode every combination of conditions as separate states instead of abstracting decisions.
Utility AI
Score and Select
  • Compute a utility score for each action from multiple considerations.
  • Actions are prioritized by numeric utility; the highest runs.
  • Flexible: add or retune considerations without refactoring flow logic.
Practical tip
Evaluate utilities at a fixed interval and only for relevant actions to reduce overhead.
Example scenario
A squad leader weighs health, enemy proximity, and reinforcements to choose between attack, heal, or retreat.
Misconception
Utility AI is not automatically smarter; it requires correct considerations and tuned curves to behave well.
Key takeaway
When choices depend on multiple graded inputs, prefer scoring over many discrete states.

screens.title: Utility AI — The core idea
screens.subtitle: Actions are scored, and the top score wins

narration.text: At the center of Utility AI is a simple claim: give every possible action a utility value that represents how desirable that action is right now, and choose the action with the highest utility. An action can be anything the agent does—attack, heal, flee, patrol. Each action's utility is computed from several considerations, which are functions that inspect the agent or environment and return a normalized score. For example, a MyHealth consideration could map currentHealth divided by maxHealth to a 0–1 value using a curve that spikes when health is low. DistanceToTarget maps distance to a score that may favor close targets for attack. There are multiple ways to combine consideration scores: multiplication emphasizes that every consideration must be favorable; averaging or weighted sums let strong considerations override weak ones. A key misunderstanding is that utilities are absolute; they are only meaningful relative to other candidate actions. So design considerations and combination rules with the full action set in mind. In practice, you will implement Consideration classes with a Score(agent) method, create AIAction objects composed of considerations, and add a Decision Maker to evaluate utilities at intervals. The result is behavior that naturally balances trade-offs and adapts to context.

keyIdea.title: Concept
keyIdea.text: Utility AI ranks candidate behaviors by computed usefulness, enabling flexible prioritization based on multiple factors.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.6 › Utility AI — Core Idea
Term
Utility
A numerical value representing how useful an action is given current game state. Compare utilities across options and execute the highest.
Action
Attack, Heal, Flee
Behaviors available to the agent.
Consideration
MyHealth, DistanceToTarget
Small functions mapping state to 0–1 scores.
Key Takeaway

Utility is relative. Tune considerations and combination rules with all actions in view to shape behavior predictably.

How it works
  1. Compute each Consideration score from agent state.
  2. Combine consideration scores to form an action utility.
  3. Compare utilities for all available actions.
  4. Execute the action with the highest utility.
Concrete example
If MyHealth gives 0.9 for Heal and DistanceToTarget gives 0.8 for Attack, multiplication might yield Heal:0.9 and Attack:0.8; the agent heals when health is critical.
Misconception: Multiplying always works. In fact, multiplication punishes any low consideration; choose combination methods that match your design goals.

screens.title: Actions, Considerations, and Scoring Functions
screens.subtitle: Defining the building blocks of Utility AI

narration.text: A Utility AI system has three primary building blocks you will use repeatedly: Actions, Considerations, and Scoring Functions. Actions are the behaviors your agent can perform, like Attack, Heal, Flee, Patrol. Each Action must expose an execution path—either a method on the agent or a delegate the Decision Maker can call. Considerations are the inputs that inform how desirable an Action is. Think of them as small sensors: MyHealth, DistanceToEnemy, AmmoCount. Each Consideration returns a normalized score, typically between zero and one. Scoring Functions map raw state values to these normalized scores. In Unity you often use AnimationCurve assets for expressive shapes, or simple math functions like linear, sigmoid, or exponential mappings. Structuring your code around these types—Action objects that contain a list of Considerations, each with a Score(agent) method—keeps data modular and tunable. An important practical point is naming: label considerations and curves in the Inspector so designers can see what each does. A common mistake is mixing execution logic into considerations; keep them pure data-to-score mappers. The clarity of these layers makes tuning and debugging far easier during playtests.

keyIdea.title: Structure
keyIdea.text: Keep Actions, Considerations, and Scoring Functions distinct: one executes behavior, one measures state, one maps values to scores.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.6 › Components
Action
Executes behavior
Contains a list of considerations and a method or delegate to run when selected.
Example: Attack action contains DistanceToTarget and EnemyHealth considerations.
Consideration
Maps state to score
A pure scoring function taking the agent as input and returning 0–1. Keep logic separate from execution.
Example: MyHealthConsideration evaluates currentHealth / maxHealth then applies a curve.
Scoring Function
Curve or math
Use AnimationCurve or a math function to shape sensitivity, threshold, and scaling for a consideration.
Tip: store curves as assets so designers can iterate without code changes.
Analogy
Considerations are sensors, scoring functions are calibrations, and actions are tools the agent can use.
Common mistake
Putting movement or execution code inside considerations. Keep them pure to simplify testing and reuse.
Check your understanding
Can you list three considerations for an Attack action? Try naming them and sketching expected curves.

narration.text: Scoring functions convert raw game values into normalized scores that reflect desirability. The shape of these functions dramatically changes how the AI reacts. Consider a MyHealth consideration for a Heal action: a curve that rises steeply near zero health will make the agent prioritize healing only when health is critical, while a gentler slope will cause earlier healing behavior. Distance considerations can be inverted or non-linear: for attack you might prefer close ranges, so the curve gives high scores at low distances; for flee you might give higher scores when the enemy is close and health is low, perhaps using a combination of two curves. Common mathematical shapes include linear ramps, exponential growth or decay, and sigmoid curves for smooth thresholds. In Unity you can express these via AnimationCurve assets for immediate designer control. A key tuning technique is normalizing input ranges—clamping distance by a reasonable maxDistance ensures the curve behaves predictably. Also watch for how you combine consideration outputs: multiplication punishes any low score and yields more conservative behavior; sums or weighted averages allow one dominant consideration to override others. Always test multiple situations so you understand how curve shapes interact across actions.

keyIdea.title: Curve effect
keyIdea.text: Curve shapes control sensitivity and thresholds—steep curves force decisive reactions near a boundary, shallow curves create gradual shifts.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.6 › Scoring Functions
Common curve types
  • Linear: predictable ramp, simple thresholding.
  • Sigmoid: smooth threshold, avoids sharp jumps.
  • Exponential: emphasizes extremes, very sensitive near one end.
Normalization matters: scale raw values into a known range (for example, distance / maxDistance) so the curve behaves consistently across agents.
Concrete example
Set MyHealth curve to produce high scores when healthNormalized is near zero for an aggressive Heal action. Use different curve shapes for Attack and Flee to create distinct decision boundaries.
Visual sampler
Steep
Responds only when value crosses a narrow threshold.
Smooth
Gradual response across a range of inputs.
Tuning tip
Use playtest traces of utility numbers while adjusting curves so you can see cause and effect.

screens.title: Combining Consideration Scores
screens.subtitle: Multiply, average, or sum—each combining rule shapes behavior differently

narration.text: Once you have normalized consideration scores, you must choose how to combine them into a single utility for an action. The three common approaches are multiplication, averaging (or weighted sum), and additive scoring. Multiplication treats considerations like gates: if any one consideration is near zero the overall utility collapses. This is useful when you want every factor to be reasonably favorable. For example, an Attack action might require both proximity and ammo; if either is zero, attack is unsuitable. Averaging or weighted sums let a strong consideration compensate for a weak one. If healing is critical, a very high MyHealth-derived score can outweigh a mediocre DistanceToTarget score. Additive models can be easiest to reason about but require careful scaling so a few large values don't dominate. Remember that chosen combination rules interact with curve shapes; a steep health curve combined with multiplication yields very defensive behavior. A misconception is assuming a single combination rule fits all actions—different actions may use different rules or weights. In practice, implement combination as a small strategy object so you can swap methods per action and tune behavior precisely during testing.

keyIdea.title: Combination matters
keyIdea.text: The method you use to combine scores directly controls whether an action requires all favorable conditions or can be driven by one strong factor.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.6 › Combining Scores
Multiply
Product of consideration scores. Use when all considerations must be reasonably true.
Effect: conservative, punishes any low score.
Weighted sum / Average
Combine with weights so important considerations carry more influence.
Effect: flexible, allows compensation between considerations.
Additive
Sum raw scores or scaled values. Simple but requires normalization so totals are comparable between actions.
Effect: intuitive but sensitive to scale.
Concrete example
Heal action: multiply(MyHealthScore, IsSafeToHealScore). If safety is zero, healing won't be chosen even with low health.
Misconception
Assuming multiplication always yields best results. It creates brittle decision boundaries if some considerations are noisy or intermittent.

screens.title: Evaluator / Decision Maker Loop
screens.subtitle: How to iterate actions and select the best option

narration.text: The Decision Maker is the runtime component that evaluates available AIAction objects and chooses which to execute. In Unity, implement this as a class or MonoBehaviour with a list of available actions and a decisionInterval to control frequency. On each evaluation tick, iterate all actions, call each consideration's Score(agent), combine the scores according to the action's combination rule, and track the highest utility. If the selected action differs from the currently executing one, switch and optionally log the change with its utility for debugging. A common implementation detail is to start with a default highestUtility of -1, then update when you find larger values. Also protect against null targets or divide-by-zero in normalization functions. For performance, avoid evaluating every consideration every frame; either evaluate on a small interval or skip irrelevant actions. The Decision Maker should keep action execution decoupled from scoring: the action exposes Execute(agent) or a delegate that runs movement, animation, or other behaviors. Finally, include debug logging of actionName and utility to watch the AI's choices during playtests and to validate that curves and weights behave as intended.

keyIdea.title: Decision loop
keyIdea.text: Evaluate all actions at controlled intervals, compute utilities, and execute the highest-scoring action while keeping scoring decoupled from execution.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.6 › Decision Maker
Core responsibilities
  • Hold a list of AIAction assets available to the agent.
  • On a fixed interval, compute utilities for each action.
  • Select and execute the highest utility action.
  • Log decisions for debugging and visualization.
Execution decoupling
Actions should expose a delegate or method the Decision Maker calls; scoring must not directly move the agent.
Snippet (conceptual)
// Pseudocode concept: Evaluate actions every decisionInterval float highest = -1; AIAction best = null; foreach action in actions: float u = action.GetUtility(agent); if u > highest: highest = u; best = action; if best != current: switch to best and log utility;
Debug tip: Print actionName and utility with two decimal places so you can correlate curve adjustments with runtime choices.

screens.title: Consideration ScriptableObjects in Unity
screens.subtitle: How to make MyHealth and DistanceToTarget reusable assets

narration.text: In Unity, a practical pattern is to implement considerations as ScriptableObject assets. Each Consideration class exposes a Score(agent) method and holds any needed parameters such as AnimationCurve and maxDistance. This lets designers tweak curves in the Inspector without recompiling code. For example, MyHealthConsideration stores a scoreCurve and computes healthNormalized as currentHealth divided by maxHealth; it returns scoreCurve. Evaluate(healthNormalized). DistanceToTargetConsideration can store maxDistance and its own curve, compute normalizedDistance by clamping distance / maxDistance, and evaluate the curve. Keep the classes pure: they should not move the agent or inspect unrelated systems. A crucial implementation detail is guarding against divide-by-zero when maxHealth is zero, and returning zero when a target is null. Use CreateAssetMenu attributes to make asset creation simple from the Project window. This pattern improves reuse: the same Consideration asset can be shared across several actions or agents, and you can compose different combinations of considerations for each AIAction. When tuning, prefer adjusting curves in the Inspector while you run the scene to observe score logs in real time. Consideration ScriptableObjects in Unity means using scriptableobjects for considerations makes curves and parameters editable for designers and reusable across actions and agents.. In practical terms, how to make myhealth and distancetotarget reusable assets. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: ScriptableObjects benefit
keyIdea.text: Using ScriptableObjects for considerations makes curves and parameters editable for designers and reusable across actions and agents.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.6 › Consideration ScriptableObjects
Pattern benefits
  • Editable curves and parameters in the Inspector.
  • Reuse the same Consideration across actions or agents.
  • Designer-friendly iteration without code changes.
Implementation note: add safe guards like returning 0 when target is null or max values are zero to avoid runtime errors.
Conceptual code
public class MyHealthConsideration : Consideration { public AnimationCurve scoreCurve; public override float Score(AIAgent agent) { if (agent.maxHealth == 0) return 0; float healthNormalized = agent.currentHealth / agent.maxHealth; return scoreCurve.Evaluate(healthNormalized); } }
Create asset menus to let designers make and reuse these assets easily from the Editor.

screens.title: AIAction and Execution Wiring
screens.subtitle: Compose considerations and connect behavior methods

narration.text: An AIAction groups a name, a list of Consideration assets, and a reference to executable logic. In Unity the AIAction ScriptableObject holds a List and an Action ExecuteAction delegate. During agent initialization you wire known action names to concrete methods on the agent: if action. actionName is Attack, set ExecuteAction to a method that moves toward the player and fires. This separation keeps data in assets and execution in code, which is useful for swapping AI behaviors without changing agent code. The action’s GetUtility(agent) iterates its considerations and combines their scores using the chosen strategy, returning the final float utility. Keep ExecuteAction null-safe and idempotent when called repeatedly—many decision loops continuously call the current action while it’s active. A common pitfall is assuming ScriptableObjects can directly reference scene objects; instead, pass the agent instance into Score and Execute so assets remain reusable across scenes and agents. Finally, add logging in GetUtility during early testing to record each consideration’s contribution so you can see how the final utility was formed. AIAction and Execution Wiring means store action composition in assets and execution on the agent; wire them at runtime for flexibility and reuse.. In practical terms, compose considerations and connect behavior methods. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Separation of concerns
keyIdea.text: Store action composition in assets and execution on the agent; wire them at runtime for flexibility and reuse.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.6 › AIAction
What an AIAction contains
  • actionName for identification.
  • List of Consideration ScriptableObjects.
  • ExecuteAction delegate or reference to an agent method.
Design tip: Provide descriptive action names so wiring code can map names to agent methods clearly and safely.
Conceptual code
public class AIAction : ScriptableObject { public string actionName; public List<Consideration> considerations; public Action<AIAgent> ExecuteAction; public float GetUtility(AIAgent agent) { float score = 1f; foreach(var c in considerations) score *= c.Score(agent); return score; } }
Ensure GetUtility has predictable defaults and that ExecuteAction is assigned at runtime by the agent that owns the actions.

screens.title: NPCUtilityAI — MakeDecision and Update
screens.subtitle: Driving behavior from evaluation to execution

narration.text: The NPCUtilityAI (or AIAgent) MonoBehaviour ties assets and execution together. It stores agent state—currentHealth, maxHealth, moveSpeed—and references to available AIAction assets. In Start(), wire action names to methods like Attack, Heal, and Flee so each action has an ExecuteAction. The Update loop accumulates a decisionTimer and, when it exceeds decisionInterval, calls MakeDecision. MakeDecision iterates all actions, calls GetUtility(agent) to compute utilities, and selects the highest. If the best action differs from the current one, update the active action reference and optionally log the new choice with its utility. After the decision step, continuously call the active action's execution method each frame so animations and movement keep updating. Practical considerations: pick a decision interval that balances responsiveness and performance—0.3 to 0.6 seconds is often a good starting point. Also, handle null targets gracefully and avoid expensive operations inside Score by caching values where possible. This structure yields agents that appear responsive without overtaxing C P U in complex scenes. NPCUtilityAI — MakeDecision and Update means agent code wires assets to execution methods, runs a timed decision loop, and continuously executes the chosen action for smooth behavior.. In practical terms, driving behavior from evaluation to execution. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Agent pattern
keyIdea.text: Agent code wires assets to execution methods, runs a timed decision loop, and continuously executes the chosen action for smooth behavior.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.6 › NPCUtilityAI
Key fields
  • Transform target, currentHealth, maxHealth, moveSpeed.
  • List<AIAction> availableActions assigned in the Inspector.
  • decisionInterval and a timer to control evaluation frequency.
Runtime wiring: in Start() map action names to local methods so actions call agent behaviors when selected.
Snippet (conceptual)
void Update() { decisionTimer += Time.deltaTime; if (decisionTimer >= decisionInterval) { MakeDecision(); decisionTimer = 0; } if (currentBestAction != null) currentBestAction.ExecuteAction(this); } void MakeDecision() { /* evaluate utilities and pick highest */ }
Design tip: Separating decision timing from execution keeps evaluation cheap and behavior smooth between decision ticks.

screens.title: Attack, Heal, Flee — A practical setup
screens.subtitle: How to compose considerations and set curves for three actions

narration.text: Let's ground the pattern in a concrete NPC: Attack, Heal, and Flee. For Attack, include considerations like DistanceToTarget (high score when close) and EnemyHealth (prefer to attack weakened enemies). Use a curve that favors short distances. For Heal, the key is MyHealthConsideration with a curve that returns a high score at low normalized health; you may also include IsSafeToHeal as a binary or near-binary consideration that penalizes healing under threat. For Flee, combine MyHealth (high when low) and DistanceToTarget (high when enemy is close) but consider inverting the distance curve or using a separate flee-specific curve. When you create the AIAction assets, assign these considerations and choose a combination rule: multiplication works well for Flee if both low health and close enemy must be present, while a weighted sum might be better for Attack to allow strong proximity to override a slightly low ammo count. In the Unity Editor make three ScriptableObjects, assign their curves via the Inspector, then add them to the NPC's availableActions list. Playtest and adjust curves iteratively until behavior matches design intent. Attack, Heal, Flee — A practical setup means compose considerations and choose combination rules per action so behaviors like attack, heal, and flee respond to the intended game signals.. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Example composition
keyIdea.text: Compose considerations and choose combination rules per action so behaviors like Attack, Heal, and Flee respond to the intended game signals.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.6 › Attack / Heal / Flee
Attack
Considerations: DistanceToTarget (high when close), EnemyHealth (high when enemy is weak). Combination: weighted sum to allow strong proximity to dominate.
Heal
Considerations: MyHealth (high when low), IsSafeToHeal (reduces healing if enemies are near). Combination: multiply so safety gates healing.
Flee
Considerations: MyHealth (high when low), DistanceToTarget (high when close). Combination: multiply for a decisive flee when both are true.
Practical step
Create three AIAction ScriptableObjects, set their consideration lists and curves, then assign them to the NPC's availableActions list in the Inspector.
Tuning prompt
Adjust one curve at a time, run short playtests, and log utilities to understand each change's effect before modifying another parameter.

screens.title: Debugging and Visualizing Utilities
screens.subtitle: Tools and practices to make behavior transparent

narration.text: Debugging Utility AI focuses on making invisible numbers visible. Begin by logging each action's utility and its consideration breakdown when decisions change. A simple log like 'Heal: 0.82 (MyHealth=0.91, IsSafe=0.90)' helps pin down which consideration is driving the decision. In the Editor, use custom gizmos or on-screen UI to show active utilities and the currently selected action; even simple text above the agent is valuable during tuning. For curve-based considerations, adjust AnimationCurve keys live while the game runs and watch utility traces update; this immediate feedback loop is the fastest path to sensible curves. Another technique is to temporarily expose individual consideration scores in the inspector via debug fields updated each tick. When behavior is noisy, apply smoothing or hysteresis: require a small margin before switching actions to avoid frequent toggling. Finally, keep performance in mind: heavy logging can slow your scene, so toggle verbose logs only during focused tuning sessions and profile the Decision Maker's cost when you scale actions and agents in a scene. Debugging and Visualizing Utilities means expose utilities and consideration breakdowns with logs, debug fields, and inspector traces to understand and tune behavior quickly.. screens.title: Performance and Scaling
screens.subtitle: Keep utility evaluation efficient at scale

narration.text: Utility AI can become expensive if every consideration for every action is evaluated every frame across many agents. To scale, apply several practical optimizations. First, evaluate utilities at a fixed decisionInterval rather than every frame; this reduces cost and still gives responsive behavior for most gameplay. Second, short-circuit irrelevant actions: if an action requires a target and none exists, skip computing its considerations. Third, group considerations so cheap checks can gate expensive ones. For example, check distance first before computing a heavy pathfinding-based consideration. Fourth, cache intermediate values when possible during a single decision evaluation; for example compute normalizedDistance once and reuse it across considerations. Fifth, evaluate only a subset of actions if you can define relevance filters based on context. Remember that premature optimization is unnecessary—start with a straightforward implementation, measure with the Unity profiler, and then apply targeted optimizations where the profiler shows hotspots. Finally, consider staggering decision ticks among agents so not every agent evaluates in the same frame, smoothing C P U usage across frames. Decision Interval
Evaluate utilities every 0.3–0.6s instead of each frame for many agents to reduce CPU cost while maintaining responsiveness.
Relevance checks
Skip actions whose preconditions are not met, e.g., actions that require a target when none exists.
Gating & caching
Compute cheap checks first, cache normalized inputs, and avoid recalculating expensive values across considerations.
Scaling tip
Stagger decision ticks across agents and profile to find hotspots before optimizing. Maintain readable debug hooks for tuning after optimizations.

narration.text: We close with compact definitions to anchor your memory. First, Utility AI is a framework where actions are scored by their usefulness in the current state and the highest score is selected. Second, a Consideration is a measurable factor—like health or distance—that maps state to a normalized score, typically via a curve or function. Third, a Scoring Function is the curve or mathematical mapping that transforms a raw input into that normalized value. These three ideas are the essential vocabulary you will use when designing and implementing Utility AI systems. Keep them distinct in your mind: action equals behavior, consideration equals sensor-to-score, and scoring function equals the calibration that shapes sensitivity and thresholds. Being precise with these terms will help you communicate with designers and programmers while tuning behavior in your projects.

narration.text: Finish by remembering three operational ideas and a practical trade-off. First, the Utility Score is the combined numeric value representing an action's desirability at a moment. Second, the Decision Maker is the component that computes utilities, compares them, and triggers the chosen action. Third, ScriptableObject is a Unity pattern for storing considerations and actions as editable assets, enabling designer iteration without code changes.
